script.text: Why is the EPR paradox weird?
Take a pair of entangled particles, and send one of them off to Alpha Centauri.
When Alice measures her particle, Bob's particle becomes known, even though Bob hasn't measured it yet.
And they claim it for sure wasn't known before Alice measured. Oh no. Before that, it was in an unknowable state.
And they're like, "That's so mysterious, right?" And I'm like, why wasn't it known all along?
Well, here's why it couldn't have been known all along. We'll explain it with three increasingly true lies.
The first lie goes like this. Alice and Bob bump a phone app that gives them each a button. Pressing it shows a zero or a one.
And the app claims that, mysteriously, they'll see the same number, even if they press the button a light-year apart.
But why couldn't the app just assign each phone the same number when they bump?
OK, fair enough. On to the second lie. Now the app has two buttons, and pressing either one removes both buttons, and shows a zero or a one.
The claim is that if they press the same button, they'll see the same number, but if they press different buttons, they'll see different numbers. Even a light-year apart!
But again, why couldn't the app assign a number to each button when they bump? The same on both phones, and a different number to each button.
Then the prediction works out no matter what they each decide to press.
OK, fine. On to the third, and nearly final, lie. Now the app has three buttons, stacked like a traffic light.
And now it claims that whatever they press, they'll get the same number, unless one person presses the top button and the other presses the bottom button. Then they'll get different numbers.
Now it really is tricky. When the phones bump, what can the app assign?
If it assigns a one to the top button, then it needs a one on the middle button too, in case one person presses top and the other presses middle.
